title: Debt
hook: owing weighs on a soul; the Church prays for relief
tomorrow: how does a farmer with full barns end up called a fool?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tithe: giving to the Church and the poor off the top, before the bills. The line was give first. Now the other column of the ledger.

A payment app sends a friendly reminder. A statement sits unopened on the counter. Owing has a weight, even when the number is small. Jesus tells a story about a man under a weight nobody could lift. A servant is brought before his king, owing ten thousand talents. The king orders him sold, with his wife and his children and all he has, to pay it. The man falls to the floor and begs for patience, promising to pay it all. And the king…
screen: `A REMINDER, UNOPENED.` → `TEN THOUSAND TALENTS.` → `HAVE PATIENCE WITH ME.`

segments.voice: …lets him go. Not a payment plan. In the Douay-Rheims Bible, the lord, moved with pity, "let him go and forgave him the debt." All of it. Then the same servant walks out and finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred pence. He seizes him by the throat: "Pay what thou owest." The man begs in nearly the words the servant himself had just used. No mercy. Into prison. When the king hears, he asks the question the whole story turns on: "Shouldst not thou then have had compassion also on thy fellow servant, even as I had compassion on thee?" That's the Lord's Prayer told as a story. In Matthew's version: "forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." Luke's version says sins, then forgives every one that is indebted. Sin is pictured as owing, and mercy as a debt written off, first received and then passed on. That is why the two halves of the line come tied together. The Church means real money too. The law of Moses ordered a remission of debts in the seventh year, and Saint John Paul the Second, preparing for a jubilee year, asked that the debts of poor nations be reduced or canceled. And Paul leaves exactly one debt open: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another."
screen: `THE KING FORGIVES ALL OF IT.` · `A HUNDRED PENCE, BY THE THROAT.` · `SIN PICTURED AS OWING.` · `OWE NOTHING BUT LOVE.` · then, large: `FORGIVE US OUR DEBTS.`

segments.voice: Bring one debt to mind, money or otherwise: a bill, a loan from a friend, a favor never returned. Name it plainly, then choose the next small step and the day you'll take it. If you pray, you can pray for someone carrying a debt heavier than yours, and for the people they owe.
Debt. What's owed, in money or in mercy, and in Matthew's prayer, what's asked to be forgiven, as it is forgiven to others.
Keep this one: forgive us our debts, the hundred pence let go the way the ten thousand talents were. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1639 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOW DOES A FARMER WITH FULL BARNS END UP CALLED A FOOL?`

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Lord's Prayer daily and at every Mass, asking forgiveness as they forgive; the Church has also called for relief of the debts of poor nations, notably ahead of a jubilee year.

myth: 'trespasses' is the word in Matthew's text of the prayer
Matthew has debts; Luke has sins. trespasses is the wording of the prayer as it's said in English at Mass.
in the story, the king gives the servant a payment plan
he forgives the whole debt and lets him go.
the law of Moses ordered a remission of debts in the seventh year
Deuteronomy 15. debt was never only a private matter.

fork.setup: your cousin quietly forgot the $40 you owed her. now your little brother owes you $5, and you're about to hound him for it. what does the story put first?
options: remember what was let go for you before you collect from him.
collect: the story is about paying back what you owe.
let it go only if he begs the way you would have.
fork.reveal: the servant's sin wasn't asking for money; it was forgetting his own forgiven debt with his hands on his fellow servant's throat.

original.note: Greek: debts, things owed. Matthew's word in the Lord's Prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: debts in the Lord's Prayer is just an old word for sins.
what it means: Matthew pictures sin as owing and mercy as a debt written off, received and then passed on.
what a scholar hears: one picture runs from the seventh-year remission in Deuteronomy 15 to the ten thousand talents of Matthew 18.
guess: what's owed, in money or in mercy
a promise made to God at Mass
a fine the Church charges for sins
recall: giving off the top, before the bills

chat.says: still owe mia $80 for my cleats from the fall. she never mentions it. why's it feel heavier?
options: Owing weighs even when it's quiet. Name it with her and set a plan; keep only love owed.
Because she's secretly mad. Pay it all at once or just never bring it up.
It only counts if she asks. Wait until she needs the money back.
chat.meaning: Paul says owe no one anything but love. A debt named with a next step is lighter than one hidden; it's still owed either way.

talents.meaning: a large unit of money in the ancient world

pence.meaning: small coins, in the Douay-Rheims wording of the story

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old English Catholic translation of the Bible

jubilee year.meaning: a holy year of mercy and pilgrimage the Church proclaims

John Paul the Second.meaning: a pope, now honored by Catholics as a saint

notes: Douay-Rheims Matthew 18:27, 18:28 ('Pay what thou owest'), 18:33, Matthew 6:12 and Romans 13:8 quoted from memory; confirm exact Challoner wording.

Matthew 18:23–35 retold: ten thousand talents, sold with wife and children, begs for patience (18:26), a hundred pence, seized by the throat (DR 'throttled'), prison, the king's question. Confirm the retelling.
Luke 11:4 paraphrased: 'forgive us our sins, for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us.' Confirm.
Deuteronomy 15:1–2: remission of debts in the seventh year; confirm paraphrase.

Tertio Millennio Adveniente 51: John Paul II, preparing the Great Jubilee, proposed reducing substantially, if not cancelling outright, the international debt of poor nations. Paraphrased without the year; confirm.
Myth item: 'trespasses' as the English Mass wording of the prayer (Matthew 6:12 has 'debts'). Confirm the reveal's phrasing for the US Missal.
Practice kind: a plan (next step). Outline practice 'pay down one thing, or pray for debtors' offered as an invitation.
